planting.note: Overseed into an established stand of native bunchgrass in fall, since seedlings must attach to grass roots as a partial parasite to grow vigorously.

directions: Overseed into an established stand of native bunchgrass in fall, since seedlings must attach to grass roots as a partial parasite to grow vigorously; sowing bare paintbrush seed alone in fertile garden soil will disappoint. Native to calcareous prairies from the Edwards Plateau north into the Cross Timbers, it is longer-lived than the familiar annual Texas Indian paintbrush and blooms in shades from yellow to orange, red, or purple depending on variety. Its tubular flowers are an important early hummingbird and long-tongued bee resource in Hill Country and adjacent Gulf Coast prairie plantings. Keep it in lean, well-drained calcareous soil and resist fertilizing, which favors the host grass over the paintbrush.

planting.note: Sow onto rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in fall, mimicking limestone glades and rocky prairies.

directions: Sow onto rocky, alkaline, well-drained soil in fall, mimicking the limestone glades and rocky prairies where this gumweed naturally grows across a range spanning Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Alabama. Its resinous flower buds open into bright yellow daisy flowers from summer into fall, offering a reliable late nectar source for native bees and butterflies when many spring bloomers have finished. As a biennial to short-lived perennial it forms a basal rosette the first year before flowering and setting seed, then it self-sows readily in disturbed, sunny ground. It tolerates poor, thin soils and heat well, making it a low-input choice for rocky Gulf South wildflower plantings.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Direct-sow into sandy, well-drained soil in spring, siting in longleaf pine sandhills, turkey-oak ridges, or similar disturbed conditions.

directions: Direct-sow into sandy, well-drained soil in spring, siting it in the longleaf pine sandhills, turkey-oak ridges, or disturbed roadside conditions it favors from east Texas and Louisiana across the Gulf Coastal Plain to Florida. The soft, hairy-leaved rosette sends up branching stems bearing yellow daisy flowers with a chocolate-tinted, papery green calyx that persists after bloom, giving the plant its common name. Its nectar and pollen support a range of native bees and butterflies through a long summer bloom season. It is closely related to Texas greeneyes but is better adapted to the sandy, humid conditions of the coastal plain rather than the drier Hill Country and West Texas range of its cousin.

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare, well-drained soil in fall so plants can form a branching rosette before flowering in spring.

directions: Broadcast seed onto bare, well-drained soil in fall so plants can form a branching rosette before producing masses of small yellow daisies in spring, often carpeting sandy Texas fields alongside bluebonnets and other winter annuals. Unlike its perennial relative Tetraneuris scaposa, this species is a true annual that reseeds itself each year given open, undisturbed ground. It is a reliable early nectar and pollen source for small native bees and beneficial flies emerging in late winter and early spring across Texas prairies. Keep it in lean, dry soil, since fertile or overwatered beds crowd this low, fine-textured wildflower out.

planting.note: Surface-sow in fall and leave uncovered, since seed needs light to germinate.

directions: Surface-sow in fall across the eastern two-thirds of Texas, Louisiana, and the broader Gulf South, where it germinates as a winter rosette and sends up wiry stems topped with small white to pale-pink, yellow-centered daisies from late spring into summer. It is one of the earliest and most dependable native nectar sources for small bees, syrphid flies, and butterflies in disturbed fields, roadsides, and open meadows. Left unmowed, it self-sows freely without becoming weedy in most garden settings, and its fine, airy texture makes a good filler among coarser prairie perennials. It tolerates average to slightly moist soils and light, sandy loam typical of Gulf Coast lowlands.
